questions.q: What does [row["order_id"] for row in orders if row["status"] == "Shipped"] produce?
options: A dictionary mapping order_id to status
A list of every field in each shipped row
A list of order_id values, only for rows where status is 'Shipped'
A single order_id value
questions.explain: This is a list comprehension that transforms and filters orders in one line.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a list comprehension, in order?
options: The filter condition, the import statement, and the return value
The function definition, the loop, and the print statement
The variable name, the data type, and the default value
The expression to produce, the loop over the collection, and the optional filter condition
questions.explain: A comprehension reads as: expression — for item in collection — if condition.

questions.q: What does a dict comprehension like {row["order_id"]: total for row in orders} build?
options: A single combined total for all orders
A dictionary keyed by order_id, mapping each to its total
A list of tuples
A set of unique order IDs
questions.explain: A dict comprehension produces key-value pairs, here keyed by order_id.

questions.q: Why is a dict keyed by order_id more useful than a plain list of order rows for repeated lookups?
options: Dictionaries can only hold numbers, making lookups faster
A dictionary lookup by key is immediate, instead of scanning the whole list each time
There is no actual performance or usability difference
Lists cannot contain more than one item
questions.explain: Looking up a key in a dict avoids scanning every item, unlike searching a list for a matching value.

questions.q: When is a regular for loop generally a better choice than a comprehension?
options: Whenever more than one item needs to be processed
Only when working with strings, never with dictionaries
When the logic involves multiple steps, multiple conditions, or side effects like printing or logging
Comprehensions should always be preferred, with no exceptions
questions.explain: Comprehensions are best for simple transform-and-filter logic; complex logic is clearer as a loop.
